For some women, being unable to access a shower, bath or birth pool at their local hospital was a sig-nificant issue. These women viewed warm water or water immersion as a very important pain relief alternative to the pharmacological options (J Coburn and Doering, 2021; Rigg et al., 2017; de Oliveira Sanfelice and Shimo, 2016). As one participant explained; “Birth in water is so ok yet it’s so not achievable in standard hospitals. Labouring and birthing in the shower is almost unheard of [in my country].” (Rigg et al., 2017).Safety is a safe care modelThis theme only represents women who chose to have midwifery care for their home birth. These women reported feeling safer in their choice to birth at home because they had one to one care with a midwife, or with a very small number of midwives, that was/were known to them and that were seen at every care episode (Bernhard et al., 2014; Boucher et al., 2009; Catling et al., 2014; Cheyney, 2008; J Coburn and Doering, 2021; Holten et al., 2018; Jouhki et al., 2017; Lindgren and Erlandsson, 2010; Murray-Davis et al., 2014; Murray-Davis et al., 2012; Shaw and Kitzinger, 2005; Tajuddin et al., 2020; Worman-Ross and Mix, 2013; Rigg et al., 2017; Leon-Larios et al., 2019; Catling-Paull et al., 2011; Skrondal et al., 2020; Lindgren et al., 2010). Women reported a perception that this model of care is better and safer than the model wherein women see a different practitioner each time they have an appointment. One participant noted feeling that problems were more likely to be picked up earlier in a continuity of care model; she said, “with the care of having a one to one midwife at home… it’s probably more likely to be picked up early and have time to go to the hospital’’ (Lee et al., 2016). Women also noted that they had 24-hour support in this model and that they developed a mutual relationship with their mid-wife/midwives that was based on deep trust, love and respect. Addi-tionally, women stated that this model of care offered them postpartum care for up to six weeks after birth. “The after care was amazing, and I believe it made such a difference in adjusting to my new baby. I loved having the midwives come into my home to check us and offer caring and nurturing support and information“ (PA Janssen et al., 2009).Safety is preparation and hospital back-upWomen noted that preparation for birth at home was important for feeling safe (Catling et al., 2014; Cheyney, 2008; J Coburn and Doering, 2021; Howarth et al., 2014; Jackson et al., 2020; PA Janssen et al., 2009; Jouhki et al., 2017; Keedle et al., 2015; Lindgren and Erlandsson, 2010; Murray-Davis et al., 2012; Shaw and Kitzinger, 2005; Rigg et al., 2017; Coxon et al., 2014; Catling-Paull et al., 2011; Skrondal et al., 2020; Lindgren et al., 2010). It was common for women to mention that they prepared for labour and birth by taking care of their physical health and wellbeing. This included eating a good diet, exercising, and looking after their general well-being so that their body would labour well. “I had the opportunity to rest and go to yoga classes during the pregnancy. That helped me be in good shape for the birth and I was happy for that since my labour went on for >36 h!” (Lindgren et al., 2010).Preparing the birth space was also important by having the right equipment, such as a birth pool and the right foods. Furthermore, women birthing at home with a midwife reported feeling safe due to the midwife’s expertise and the emergency equipment they brought to the birth (Catling et al., 2014; Cheyney, 2008; J Coburn and Doering, 2021; Howarth et al., 2014; Jackson et al., 2020; PA Janssen et al., 2009; Jouhki et al., 2017; Keedle et al., 2015; Murray-Davis et al., 2012; Catling-Paull et al., 2011; Skrondal et al., 2020). Those who had decided on freebirthing also discussed gathering equipment such as basic resuscitation equipment for the baby and educating themselves on how to use it (Jackson et al., 2020; Jackson et al., 2012; Rigg et al., 2017).Women who did organise to birth at home with a midwife frequently reported that they had planning meetings for the birth with their partner and midwife, in which they would discuss reasons to transfer to hospital. Some participants said having the safety-net of the hospital as back-up for any emergencies contributed to them feeling safe to give birth at home (Catling et al., 2014; Howarth et al., 2014; Keedle et al., 2015; Murray-Davis et al., 2012; Rigg et al., 2017; Catling-Paull et al., 2011; Skrondal et al., 2020; J Coburn and Doering, 2021) as noted by one participant: “…the option to actually go to the hospital at any time that I felt unsafe or insecure or whatever … that was beautiful …” (Catling et al., 2014).Safety is educationWomen often reported going to great lengths to educate themselves on pregnancy, labour and birth and their options (Boucher et al., 2009; Catling et al., 2014; Cheyney, 2008; Hauck et al., 2020; Holten et al., 2018; Jackson et al., 2020; PA Janssen et al., 2009; Jouhki et al., 2017; Lindgren and Erlandsson, 2010; Tajuddin et al., 2020; Worman-Ross and Mix, 2013; Rigg et al., 2017; Jouhki, 2012; Catling-Paull et al., 2011; Skrondal et al., 2020). Being educated on pregnancy, labour and birth enabled women to feel like they were making decisions that were truly informed and were best for them. One woman stated; “The decision to opt for a homebirth is one that myself and partner put a lot of thought and research into.” (Hauck et al., 2020). Many women described feeling the need to both assess and understand the risks (as they perceived them). “I think the decisions to research and understand risk and act in what you see as your best interest in understanding them… so that taking that control, understanding the risks, making those decisions I think is really important…” (Keedle et al., 2015).Women reported accessing education through the internet, books, research papers, homebirth groups and from their midwife; “[My mid-wife’s] practice was evidence based—able to answer questions refer-encing latest research. She was aware of, able to direct us to further reading.” (PA Janssen et al., 2009).DiscussionIn this systematic review we analysed research originating from 12 different countries that represent the voices of 2476 women. The study is limited by the fact that in each study, the research represented a rela-tively small number of women, and that the findings only reflect high- income maternity care contexts and an educated, literate population that has the privilege of choice and access to the resources to inform their choice. Nonetheless, the review provides a useful addition to what is already known about how women who choose to pursue home birth, with or without health care professional presence, characterise risk and safety in relation to childbirth. Furthermore, much of the existing literature focuses on women’s experiences of homebirth, birthplace preferences, or maternal and infant outcomes, fewer studies explore how women personally perceive risk and safety in birth. This review specif-ically addresses this topic.Risk in obstetrics is mostly presented as a statistical probability, e.g., 1 in 100,000. However, these types of statistics are rarely discussed in reverse when assessing risk in maternity care. Kahneman (Kahneman, 2011) writes that if we decide there is a 30 % chance of something happening, we must also hold in our minds that there is a 70 % chance that same thing won’t happen. The reality is that giving birth in devel-oped nations has never been safer as it is today: in Australia, maternal mortality rates sit at 5–6 in every 100,000 births (PA QSR International Pty Ltd 2023). When birth at home is well integrated into healthcare systems, as it is in The Netherlands, for example, it is a very safe option (Galková et al., 2022). Despite this, some women choose to opt out of organized maternity care altogether, perceiving its risks as outweighing its benefits. As the review demonstrates, risk and safety are inherently subjective, shaped by individual experiences and perspectives, which C. Chauncy et al.                                                                                                                                                                                                                               Midwifery 144 (2025) 10434010ultimately influence the decision-making process.Beck (Beck, 1992) and Kahneman (Kahneman, 2011) both wrote on the identification and interpretation of risk as an exercise in power. In contemporary Australia, health care institutions are the identifiers and interpreters of risk in relation to childbirth and thus hold the balance of power in this space. This power is then used to introduce, legislation, systems, policy, procedures, and institutions (Beck, 1992), and alter-native determinations of risk have not historically been accepted or provided for. By choosing to birth at home women are reclaiming power and control and, as Cheyney (2008) (Cheyney, 2008) wrote, actively challenging established and authoritative ways of knowing.ConclusionThis review demonstrated that women who choose homebirth assess risk and safety through a different socio-cultural framework to that used by healthcare institutions. Our findings highlight the need for health professionals to be aware that women will assess risks from their own experiences and socio-cultural frameworks. Policies and procedures that centre a human rights-based approach would support accommodation of different risk constructs in maternity care settings, and offering midwifery continuity of care models would offer a way for maternity services to deliver such an approach. Finally, further research is rec-ommended into what safety and risk means to women in relation to birth more generally.CRediT authorship contribution statementCandice Chauncy: Writing – review & editing, Writing – original draft, Conceptualization. Despite the availability of policies targeted at 5 this age group, policy formulation, implementation, and gains in adolescent health continue to be 6 underwhelming.  Actors or stakeholders are architects of policy, bringing their ideological values, 7 interests, power, and positions to policy formulation and implementation and thus influencing the policy 8 process.  We analysed multi-level stakeholder interests, positions, power and their influence on 9 adolescent sexual, reproductive and mental health policy formulation and implementation in Ghana, 10 West Africa, using a single-case study design with multiple embedded sub-units of analysis.  The case 11 was defined as actors, their power, interests, positions, and the influence on policy formulation and 12 implementation processes in adolescent sexual, reproductive and mental health. A conceptual 13 framework of conflict and synergies between stakeholder interests, power, and positions and the 14 influence on policy formulation and implementation was used to guide the analysis.  Data was obtained 15 from key informant in-depth interviews with 18 global and national level and 16 sub-national level 16 stakeholders; 4 focus group discussions with district health management teams, 9 with frontline health 17 workers and 20 with in and out of school adolescents in four districts in the Greater Accra region of 18 Ghana.  The multiple stakeholders in adolescent health, including adolescents themselves, had 19 sometimes synergistic and sometimes divergent and conflicting views on policy agendas, formulation 20 and approaches to implementation. Title: Socioeconomic Status and Academic Motivation: A Meta-Analysis and Systematic Review grounded on Self-Determination Theory
Text source: abstract
Evidence text:
This systematic review and meta-analysis focus on the relationship between socioeconomic status (SES) and academic motivation, grounded in self-determination theory, among elementary to high school students. SES has been studied extensively both as a predictor of academic achievement and student well-being and alternatively, as a moderator between motivation and academic achievement. Still, no metanalysis has assessed the direct effect of SES on academic motivation.
SES is assessed using different indicators, such as highest parents' educational attainment, parents’ occupation, or family income. There’s no consensus on how SES should be calculated, therefore studies differ in how they measure it. Hence, this systematic review and metanalysis aims to investigate all the different ways that SES has been measured in studies about academic motivation, and whether the choice of some indicators, instead of others, can moderate the relationship between SES and motivation.
Furthermore, this meta-analysis aims to asses potential differences of the effect of SES on academic motivation in students from elementary, middle and high school
