May. 2025Abstract: 1 Background: 2 Coeliac disease is an autoimmune disorder resulting from the consumption of gluten in genetically 3 susceptible individuals. Current treatment is a lifelong gluten-free diet that significantly affects 4 quality of life. Food-related quality of life (FRQoL) refers to the impact of food, nutrition, eating and 5 drinking on the psychosocial aspects of life. The aim of this study was to examine, FRQoL in patients 6 with coeliac disease.  7 Methods 8 Patients with confirmed coeliac disease completed the validated FR-QoL-29 questionnaire adapted 9 for coeliac disease (FR-QoL-29-Coeliac) and provided demographic and clinical information.  10 Results: 11 Questionnaires were completed by 138 adults (62% female, mean age 52.3 SD ± 18.6). FR-QoL-29 12 scores were mean 85.8 (SD ±23.1). The lowest FR-QoL-29 scores were in the 18-35 year age group 13 (76.6 ± 17.2) compared with the highest in the 56+ age-group (92.5 ± 22.3, p = 0.002). Patients with 14 ≥4 gastrointestinal (GiS) symptoms had significantly lower FR-QoL-29 scores (77.9 ± 20.7) compared 15 with those with 1-3 GiS (96.7 ± 21, p = 0.0001).  16 Conclusions: 17 FRQoL is impaired in coeliac disease and is particularly lower in younger people and those with 18 greater GI symptom burden. Further research should examine the mechanisms that reduce FRQoL 19 in coeliac disease to identify interventions that minimize the burden for patients. 20 Keywords: Coeliac Disease, Food Related Quality of Life, Gluten-Free Diet. 21  22 Key Points 23 1. Food-Related Quality of Life (FRQoL) refers to the impact of food and 24 nutrition on important psychosocial aspects of life. This includes the ability 25 to maintain social activities through eating and drinking and to achieve 26 adequate nutritional intake, whilst maintaining medically necessitated 27 dietary restrictions. 28 2. FRQoL in patients with coeliac disease is impaired, particularly in younger 29 patients and those with a higher burden of gastrointestinal symptoms. 30 3. Future research should focus on identifying mechanisms to improve FRQoL 31 through both dietetic and psychological support, with the aim of reducing 32 the treatment burden for patients with coeliac disease. 33   34 Introduction 35 Coeliac disease is an autoimmune disorder that results from the consumption of gluten in 36 genetically susceptible individuals and is increasing in both incidence and prevalence. (1) The 37 cornerstone of treatment for coeliac disease remains a strict lifelong gluten-free diet (GFD). Gluten 38 is a storage protein found in wheat, barley rye and contaminated oats. Therefore, it is contained in 39 a wide variety of foods widely distributed through the diet including bread, pastries, cakes as well 40 as many processed and packaged food products. Hence the GFD necessitates substantial dietary 41 change and rigorous adherence that represents a considerable treatment burden for many patients. 42 The aim of treatment is serological, histological, and clinical remission plus concomitant reductions 43 in associated co-morbidities including anaemia, infertility, fragility bone fracture, micronutrient 44 deficiencies and, rarely, small bowel lymphoma. (2) 45  46 Numerous studies have reported poorer health-related quality of life in children, adolescents, and 47 adults with coeliac disease and a systematic review demonstrated that although the GFD 48 significantly improves, it does not normalise, health-related quality of life in patients with coeliac 49 disease. (3,4) Furthermore patients consistently report a high associative treatment burden (‘the 50 workload of healthcare and its effect on patient functioning and well-being’) in coeliac disease 51 compared to that of other chronic conditions. Survey research indicates patients with coeliac 52 disease report the second highest treatment burden, with only renal disease reporting higher. (5,6) 53 The treatment burden of the GFD extends beyond patients with coeliac disease to their family 54 members. With more than 30% of partners experiencing mild to moderate associative burden, that 55 is directly related to the level of symptom severity of the family member with coeliac disease. (7) 56  57 Factors associated with high treatment burden in coeliac disease are related to, symptoms, disease-58 related work absences, social as well as cognitive impairments. The GFD necessitates 59 communicating dietary restrictions with food servers, family members, friends and colleagues, that 60 can make eating out and socialising challenging. Educational interventions are required to help 61 patients safely identify appropriate foods, which if not done adequately can lead to dietary over-62 restriction. In addition, shopping may be challenging as gluten-free foods are not always widely 63 available in supermarkets and the GFD can have increased financial costs, with gluten-free 64 substitute foods ranging from 4.3 to 7.2 times more expensive than standard gluten containing 65 products. (8–12)  66  67 These aspects may at least partially explain why adherence to GFD is suboptimal in adults with 68 coeliac disease, ranging between 42% and 91%. (13) Adherence has been shown to relate to a range 69 of factors, including experiences, attitudes and importantly to health-related quality of life. (14) A 70 subset of patients may experience a maladaptive response to the GFD leading to hypervigilance of 71 their food environment. Such patients experience additional psychosocial burdens in the form of 72 increased food-related anxiety, social isolation and in some cases disordered eating patterns (15–73 18) The dietary and nutritional burden of the GFD in coeliac disease has thus been a subject of 74 ongoing research with the aim to identify and mitigate potential negative consequences and 75 enhance long term dietary adherence. 76  77 Recently, the concept of food-related quality of life (FRQoL) has emerged. (19) FRQoL is related to 78 health-related quality of life and refers specifically to the impact of food and nutrition on important 79 psychosocial aspects of life. This includes the ability to maintain social activities through eating and 80 drinking and to achieve adequate nutritional intake, whilst maintaining medically necessitated 81 dietary restrictions. (19) Primarily FRQoL has been investigated in inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). 82 Research in IBD has shown that FRQoL is significantly reduced compared with healthy populations 83 and other chronic conditions. It appears to be exacerbated by the presence of active disease, 84 symptom severity, dietary misinformation and diet-related anticipatory symptom anxiety. (19,20) 85 No studies have thus far specifically investigated FRQoL in coeliac disease. 86  87 The primary outcome of this study was FRQoL-29 scores in this cohort of patients with coeliac 88 disease. The overall aim was to explore the relationship of FRQoL to age, dietary adherence to the 89 gluten-free diet (GFD), duration since diagnosis, educational attainment, presence of comorbidities, 90 and symptom burden. 91  92 Materials and Methods 93 The methodology and data collection in this study has been previously described. (21) Briefly, as the 94 National Centre for Coeliac Disease designated by NHS England, we maintain a database of over 95 3,000 patients, including demographics, referral details, and serological and histological data. 96 Approximately 10% of these patients are referrals from across England. The sample size for this 97 study was informed by prior research in a similar study, which used an a priori power analysis to 98 determine a minimum required sample size of 128 participants (22) and data collection for the 99 survey was undertaken between March 2021 to November 2021. 100  101 Adult patients with serological and histopathological confirmed coeliac disease, who had been on a 102 gluten-free diet (GFD) for at least four months, were included in the study. From our database of 103 3,000 patients, we selected a subset of 700 patients as a convenience sample based on clinic 104 attendance, aiming to represent a range of time since diagnosis. These 700 patients were contacted 105 by telephone or email to assess their interest in participation. Of these, 323 expressed interest and 106 were sent a paper-based questionnaire. Ultimately, 138 patients completed the questionnaire, 107 forming the final study cohort.  108  109 The questionnaire included the validated instruments to measure food related quality of life (FR-110 QoL_29) and adherence to the GFD (Gluten-free Diet Score (GFD-S)). (23,24) Along with questions 111 about educational attainment, comorbidities and gastrointestinal symptoms (bloating, abdominal 112 cramps, indigestion, diarrhoea, constipation, excessive flatulence or wind, excessive belching, 113 floating stools, haemorrhoids, nausea, and vomiting).  114  115 The FR-QoL-29 questionnaire was adapted to coeliac disease (FR-QoL-29-Coeliac), obtained under 116 licence from the authors. The FR-QoL-29-Coeliac is identical to the FR-QoL-29 except that the term 117 inflammatory bowel disease is replaced by coeliac disease. FR-QoL-29-Coeliac consists of 29 items 118 describing experiences of FR-QoL recorded on a 5-point Likert scale. Scores are summed (possible 119 scores ranging from 29-145). Although no cut-offs have yet been formally calculated, a score ≤90 120 has been used to indicate impaired FR-QoL. (25) 121  122 The validated Gluten-free Diet Score (GFD-S). The GFD-S consists of six questions rated via 123 dichotomous response. The sum score has five levels (0-4) that are grouped as: not following a GFD 124 (score 0-1), follow a GFD but with important errors that require correction (score 2), and follow a 125 strict GFD (score 3-4). (23) Published evidence suggests that self-management skills for adhering to 126 a GFD develop progressively over time. These skills, which range from identifying unsuitable 127 products to managing foreign travel, can take up to five years to fully develop. Therefore, the GFD-128 S scores were dichotomised based on patients with a diagnosis duration of <5 years and ≥5 years. 129 (26) 130  131 Statistical Analysis 132 Continuous demographic variables (e.g., length of diagnosis, GFD-S, symptoms, FRQoL-29) were 133 summarized as mean ± standard deviation (SD). Normality of continuous variables was assessed 134 using the Shapiro-Wilk test (p > 0.05 indicating normality). All variables met this criterion except FR-135 QoL-29 scores in participants with >4 GI symptoms (p = 0.04, W = 0.96, n = 60), where a minor 136 deviation was observed, but parametric tests were still considered appropriate. Independent t-tests 137 were used for two-group comparisons, while one-way ANOVA was used for three or more group 138 comparisons (e.g., age, presence of comorbidities), with post-hoc Bonferroni corrections where 139 required. Other demographic data were presented as percentages. A chi-square test was used to 140 compare sex differences. All analyses were conducted using MS Excel version 16.42 (Microsoft, 141 2020) and Stata/SE 18.0 (StataCorp, College Station, TX, USA), with statistical significance 142 considered at p < 0.05. 143  144  145 Ethics 146 The database is approved by the Yorkshire and Humber Research Ethics committee (REC reference 147 19/YH/0095) and registered with the local research and development department of Sheffield 148 Teaching Hospital NHS Foundation Trust (CEU ref 11075). Patients were provided with an 149 information sheet indicating that participation was voluntary and anonymous, and return of a 150 questionnaire indicated consent to participate.  151  152 Results 153  154 Of the 323 patients sent the questionnaire, 138 completed and returned a copy (43% response). 155 The demographics of the respondents are summarised in Table 1. Total FR-QoL-29 score in this 156 coeliac disease cohort was mean 85.8 (±23.1). Overall, 78 (56.5%) patients had a FR-QoL-29 score 157 ≤90 (Table 2). 158  159 Overall, FR-QoL-29 scores were not different between groups based upon length of time diagnosed 160 with coeliac disease (< 5 years 84.1 ± 12.0 vs ≥ 5 years 88.1 ± 30.4. p = 0.34) nor levels of adherence 161 in relation to the GFD-S (‘not following a GFD’ 89.1 ± 43.8 vs ‘following a strict GFD’ 84.9 ± 22.3. p 162 =0.49). FR-QoL-29 score was similarly not different between males (86.3 ± 21.7) and females (85.4 163 ± 24.0, p = 0.83) or participants that were university educated (84.3 ± 21.0) or not (86.8 ± 24.6, p = 164 0.52). Equally, FR-QoL-29 scores were not different between the occurrence of one (86.9 ± 24.0), 165 two (88.5 ± 22.7) or greater than three (79.3 ± 24.4) comorbid conditions (ANOVA p = 0.26). 166  167 The presence of gastrointestinal symptoms (GiS) was dichotomised to categories of 1 - 3 or ≥ 4 GiS. 168 FR-QoL-29 scores were higher in those with lower GI symptom burden (1-3 GiS group, 96.7 ± 21.2) 169 than in those with higher GI symptom burden (≥ 4 GiS group, 77.9 ± 20.7, p = 0.0001).  170  171 Older participants had higher FR-QoL-29 scores. Age was subdivided into three categories: 18–35 172 (76.6 ± 17.2), 36–55 (81.0 ± 25.1), and 56+ (92.5 ± 22.3) (p = 0.002, ANOVA). Bonferroni post-hoc 173 analyses revealed that participants in the 56+ age group had higher FRQoL-29 scores compared with 174 those in the 18–35 (p = 0.005) or 36–55 (p = 0.031) age categories (Figure 1). 175  176 Specific questions from the FR-QoL-29 that reflected what patients found most challenging about 177 their coeliac disease and maintenance of the GFD were: “I have felt that I need to know what is in 178 the food I am eating, due to my coeliac disease” (88.1%  agree or strongly agree) and “I have had to 179 be more aware of what I am eating due to my coeliac disease” (88.2 agree or strongly agree). In 180 addition, the reverse-scored questions “I have felt in control of what I eat and drink in relation to 181 my coeliac disease” (78.1% disagreed or strongly disagreed) and “I have been happy to eat and drink 182 around people I do not know despite my coeliac disease” (71.7% disagreed or strongly disagreed), 183 had high numbers indicating they disagreed (Table 3). 184  185 Discussion 186 The current principal treatment for coeliac disease is the complete, lifelong removal of gluten from 187 the diet. The primary goal of the GFD is to minimise both symptoms but also the comorbid risks of 188 the disease including micronutrient depletion, reduced bone density, concomitant autoimmune 189 diseases and small bowel lymphoma.(27–30)  190  191 Appropriate application of the GFD via a multidisciplinary approach, including support and follow-192 up from specialist dietitians which improves clinical outcomes in coeliac disease. (21,31) Research 193 has also focused on the associated treatment burdens and effects on patients HRQoL. (32–36) Given 194 that dietary restriction is a central tenet of coeliac disease treatment it is important to understand 195 how the GFD interacts with the psychosocial elements of quality of life.  196  197 FRQoL is an important concept that has been under-reported in coeliac disease patients. It refers to 198 the social, emotional, and psychological roles food plays in patients daily life and how these intersect 199 with dietary restrictions. (19) Food avoidance, restrictive eating and severity of disease flares have 200 been identified as contributors to reduced FRQoL in IBD and, to a lesser extent, IBS. (22,37,38)  201  202 FRQoL scores of ≤90 have been suggested as potentially indicative of impairment. Previous studies 203 have reported FRQoL scores in adults with IBD ranging from 80.8 to 91.2 during remission (37,39), 204 67 in those with active IBD, and 68 in adults with active IBS (39). This is in comparison to FRQoL 205 scores of 123 in healthy volunteers and 125.4 in adults with asthma. (19) In the current study, the 206 mean FRQoL score was 85.8, with a wide range (minimum 31; maximum 136), indicating impairment 207 comparable to that seen in adults with quiescent IBD. Furthermore, as also highlighted in the IBD 208 and IBS literature, symptom severity was associated with lower FRQoL in people living with coeliac 209 disease, with those reporting four or more gastrointestinal symptoms having significantly lower 210 mean FRQoL scores (77.9). 211  212 Up to 30% of patients with Coeliac Disease have ongoing symptoms categorized as non-responsive 213 coeliac disease (NRCD). (40) The causes of NRCD may include misdiagnosis, intestinal bacterial 214 overgrowth, coexisting IBS, refractory disease, and most commonly ongoing accidental gluten 215 ingestion. (41) However, level of adherence to the GFD was not associated with FRQoL in this patient 216 cohort. As adherence was self-reported, correlations between accidental gluten exposure, symptom 217 burden and impaired FRQoL may have not been detected, although the subjective treatment burden 218 of the GFD itself, regardless of degree of adherence, could potentially impact negatively on FRQoL.  219  220 Nevertheless, addressing coexisting gastrointestinal symptoms in patients with coeliac disease, is 221 likely an important target for improving FRQoL. Indeed, in cases of quiescent coeliac disease with 222 medically diagnosed coexisting IBS, dietitian-led Low FODMAP diet interventions have 223 demonstrated significant reductions in gastrointestinal symptoms and overall disease burden. 224 (42,43) 225 Patients age group was also significantly associated with lower FRQoL, with younger age being 226 associated with worse FRQoL. Research has indicated patients diagnosed with coeliac disease in 227 adolescence or early adult life report more food-related social anxiety and maladaptive eating 228 behaviours. This may manifest both as hypervigilance to the food environment leading to greater 229 food preoccupation, limitation of food choices and avoidance of social situations, or conversely 230 engagement in riskier eating behaviours, and intentional gluten consumption. (18,32,44,45). The 231 finding of improved FRQoL with greater age, and poorer FRQoL in younger people, has recently been 232 demonstrated in people with inflammatory bowel disease in the USA (46). The association with age 233 is unlikely to be a function of longer disease duration in older people, as FRQoL did not differ 234 between short and longer disease duration. 235  236 Lower scores on the FR-QoL-29 are indicative of reduced FRQoL, and the low average scores 237 observed in patients with coeliac disease are a concern. However, there are some experiences in 238 the questionnaire that may represent legitimate and important behaviours in coeliac disease that 239 are crucial to managing the GFD, for example ‘I have avoided having food and drink I know does not 240 agree with my coeliac disease’ (Q7) and ‘I have had to be more aware of what I am eating, due to 241 my coeliac disease’ (Q21). Interventions to improve FRQoL in coeliac disease should balance the 242 need for dietary vigilance with food as an enjoyable part of daily life, within the constraints of a GFD.  243  244 Acknowledgement of the specific challenges that GFD presents in different age groups and the use 245 of novel methods of follow-up may lead to more targeted individualised strategies that support 246 long-term adherence. (21,47) For example, online support has been trialled as an approach to 247 improve FRQoL in a previous pilot study in IBD (25). It is acknowledged in international clinical 248 guidelines that treatment of coeliac disease should be multidisciplinary, however the role of 249 specialist gastroenterology psychologists is underfunded. Further research combining dietetic and 250 psychological practice in coeliac disease and its effects on FRQoL should be undertaken. 251  252 This study has several limitations. The patient population was 95% white, which precluded analysis 253 or inferences about FRQoL across different ethnic groups. Future research should address this gap, 254 as the challenges of adhering to a GFD in minority populations are underexplored. The participant 255 response rate of 43% is recognised as suboptimal. Recruitment was likely hindered by data 256 collection coinciding with the COVID-19 pandemic, which may have discouraged participation and 257 potentially limits the generalisability of the findings to the broader coeliac population. Another 258 limitation is that GFD adherence in this study was self-reported. Incorporating additional methods 259 to assess adherence - such as dietetic review, gluten immunogenic peptide testing, or, where 260 feasible, repeat histology - could provide a more comprehensive understanding of the relationship 261 between dietary adherence and FRQoL. Equally, research has indicated that food insecurity may 262 further complicate dietary adherence in coeliac disease, with detrimental effects on nutritional 263 adequacy. (48) The economic burden of the GFD and its implications for FRQoL remain important 264 areas for further investigation. Finally, the FR-QoL-29 questionnaire, while validated for IBD 265 populations, has not been validated for patients with coeliac disease. Although it has been applied 266 in its current form to studies evaluating other GI conditions, such as IBS and eosinophilic 267 oesophagitis, its relevance and validity for the coeliac population require further adaptation and 268 validation. (22,49) 269 In conclusion FR-QoL is impaired in coeliac disease patients and comparable to other 270 gastrointestinal disorders. Length of diagnosis and dietary adherence to the GFD did not affect FR-271 QoL in this cohort, however both the age of patients and the number of concomitant 272 gastroenterological symptoms did have an effect. Further research should examine the mechanisms 273 of action that reduce FR-QoL in coeliac disease. This could help identify the development of 274 nutritional, psychological and societal interventions to minimize the nutritional treatment burden 275 for patients with coeliac disease. 276   277 References 278 1. Jacobs, MD11, Massimo Padalino, MD, PhD12, and Vladimiro Vida, MD, PhD13AbstractBackground: Minimally invasive thoracotomies to repair selected congenital heart defects are considered only a cosmetic alter-native approach by many; however, they represent the routine alternative in centers of expertise. Methods: Pooled institutionaldata from the European Congenital Heart Surgeons Association using mini-thoracotomy approaches were analyzed since thebeginning of their respective experiences until an inclusion surgical date of January 31, 2024, allowing at least six months post-operative follow-up. Results: From 1999 to 2024, 3,007 patients from 11 centers underwent surgery. Age and weight rangedfrom 4 days to 73 years and 3.1 to 106 kg, respectively. Repaired defects included atrial and ventricular septal defects, partialanomalous pulmonary venous return, partial and complete atrioventricular septal defects, double-chambered right ventricle,cor triatriatum, scimitar syndrome, subaortic stenosis, and total anomalous pulmonary venous return (TAPVR). There was nosurgical mortality or intraoperative conversion to sternotomy. Complications included wound infections (0.59%), pacemakerrequirement (0.23%), phrenic nerve injury (0.26%), bleeding requiring exploration (0.13%), and neurologic injury (0.29%).Early or late reoperations were needed in 0.73%. Conclusion: Minimally invasive thoracotomies are the preferred approachfor selected congenital heart defects in the participating pediatric heart centers. Mini-thoracotomy incisions allow safe accessto an ever-expanding spectrum of quality repairs, low morbidity, superior cosmetics, and early return to functionality in infants,children, and adults.1 Klinik für Kinderherzchirurgie und Chirurgie angeborener Herzfehler, University Hospital RWTH Aachen, Aachen, Germany2 Pediatric Cardiac Surgery, Hospital Gregorio Marañón, Madrid, Spain3 Pediatric and Congenital Heart Surgery, German Heart Centre Munich, Munich, Germany4Congenital Cardiothoracic Surgery, University Medical Center Groningen, Groningen, the Netherlands5Department of Pediatric Cardiac Surgery, University Children’s Hospital, Zurich, Switzerland6Congenital Cardiac Surgery, IRCCS Policlinico San Donato, Milan, Italy7 Inselspital, Universität Bern, Bern, Switzerland8Cardiac surgery, Ukrainian Children’s Heart Center, Kyiv, Ukraine9 Institut Cardiovasculaire, Université Catholique de Louvain, Brussels, Belgium10Westchester Medical Center, Maria Fareri Children’s Hospital, Valhalla, NY, USA11 ECHSA Congenital Database, Warsaw, Poland12Department of Precision and Regenerative Medicine and Jonic Area, University of Bari, Bari, Italy13Department of Cardiac, Thoracic and Vascular Sciences, University of Padova Medical School, Padova, ItalyOn behalf of the Minimal Invasive Surgery Working Group of the European Congenital Heart Surgeons Association (ECHSA).Corresponding Author:Ali Dodge-Khatami, Klinik für Kinderherzchirurgie und Chirurgie angeborener Herzfehler, University Hospital RWTH Aachen, Pauwelsstrasse 30, 52074 Aachen,Germany.Email: adodgekhatam@ukaachen.deOriginal ArticleWorld Journal for Pediatric andCongenital Heart Surgery2025, Vol. 16(5) 578-584© The Author(s) 2025Article reuse guidelines:sagepub.com/journals-permissionsDOI: 10.1177/21501351251322155journals.sagepub.com/home/pchKeywordsMinimally invasive, congenital heart defects, thoracotomy, safetySubmitted November 22, 2024; Accepted January 31, 2025.Meeting presentation: 38th EACTS Annual Meeting; October 9-12, 2024; Lisbon, PortugalIntroductionReducing surgical trauma with increasingly smaller incisionsand avoiding a full median sternotomy has long been adoptedby our adult cardiac surgery colleagues,1,2 whose vast mini-mally invasive experience has become an established normand is included in the surgical training curriculum. Throughenhanced media exposure, the approach is also gaining momen-tum within the pediatric sphere, among referring cardiologists,parents, and patients alike. However, there is still reluctance formini-thoracic approaches to be fully incorporated into the dailyarmamentarium of pediatric and congenital heart surgeons sinceit is not an integrated part of the training curriculum. It isoften offered only for “simple” defects such as atrial septaldefect (ASD) closure, only in certain centers, and only by spe-cific surgeons—but why? As the current generation learns toapproach the heart only by using a sternal saw, the trepidationtoward any other access is understandable. Yet mini-thoracicapproaches are appealing for reasons beyond the obvious cos-metic advantages. The functional components and integrity ofthe thoracic cage, the cornerstone of which is the sternum, aremaintained.3 Recognized decades ago by our thoracic surgerycolleagues, mini-thoracic incisions are not only cosmeticallyappealing but lead to enhanced recovery and a quicker returnto functionality.4–6 As such, mini-thoracic incisions serve areal quality of life purpose which can and perhaps should beoffered to all patients, if their congenital heart defect anatomypermits it. The current multicenter European Congenital HeartSurgeons Association (ECHSA) experience with over 3,000patients illustrates the quality of results, and the broadeningspectrum of defects and repair types which can be achievedthrough mini-thoracic incisions.Patients and MethodsThis retrospective multi-institutional study was submitted toand approved by the ECHSA Research Committee (June 26,2023, and September 9, 2023, respectively). All participatingcenters received their local IRB approval to collect and shareanonymized retrospective observational data, and parent/patient informed consent was waived.Patient demographics and perioperative surgical data wereanalyzed from 3,007 patients undergoing primary repair usingcardiopulmonary bypass (CPB) through a mini-thoracotomyincision, operated on between 1999 and a closing enrollmentdate of January 31, 2024, with a minimum postoperativefollow-up time of six months. Defect and repair types wereselected by each center/surgeon according to their own experi-ence and comfort levels, with no specific inclusion or exclusioncriteria applied across the board. Results are given in mean±standard deviation and/or median and range when relevant.ResultsThe analysis included 3,007 patients from 11 centers. Medianage at surgery was 5.4 years, range 4 days to 73 years.Median weight was 18.9 kg, range 3.1 to 106 kg. Femalepatients represented 56.5% (n = 1700/3007) of the patient pop-ulation, prematurity was present in 4.7% (n= 102/2,166 avail-able), and chromosomal anomalies in 4.5% (n= 97/2,172reported). Primary diagnoses and repair types are given inTables 1 and 2. Central Image: Minimally Invasive Surgery Working Group of the European Congenital Heart Surgeons Association (ECHSA) andparticipating centers for the study.Dodge-Khatami et al 581by 22 different surgeons in various settings reports on qualityrepairs with no mortality, no need for intraoperative conversionto sternotomy, and a very low incidence of unplanned reopera-tions for residuals or complications. Although induced ventricular fibrillation has beenaround for a very long time prior to the advent of cardioplegia,28it has unfortunately disappeared from the regular classic train-ing curriculum. Therefore, many younger surgeons are eitherunaware or uncomfortable with it, feeling unable to operate inthe absence of an aortic cross-clamp. There is indeed a learningcurve required for induced VF and the additional de-airingmaneuvers prior to defibrillating, which are however out-weighed by its advantages once a comfort level has beenreached.29 It is critical to surgically secure continuous contactbetween the probe or wire and the heart prior to de-airingmaneuvers, as unwanted premature spontaneous defibrillationfrom loss of contact may potentially lead to devastating airembolism and complications. In 23.7% (715/3007) of cases someform of peripheral cannulation; that is, femoral or iliac arteries orveins, or more rarely percutaneous internal jugular vein cannula-tion was used. There is neither controlgroup nor generalized inclusion or exclusion criteria to deter-mine suitability for the minimally invasive approach,compared with treatment for the same defects through mediansternotomy or by percutaneous device closure. This takesaway the denominator for each defect type in each center andthroughout the collective, which was not addressed as an epide-miologic question to the centers. Title: Capturing SNP Association across the NK Receptor and HLA Gene Regions in Multiple Sclerosis by Targeted Penalised Regression Models
Text source: abstract
Evidence text:
Conventional genome-wide association studies (GWASs) of complex traits, such as Multiple Sclerosis (MS), are reliant on per-SNP p-values and are therefore heavily burdened by multiple testing correction. Thus, in order to detect more subtle alterations, ever increasing sample sizes are required, while ignoring potentially valuable information that is readily available in existing datasets. To overcome this, we used penalised regression incorporating elastic net with a stability selection method by iterative subsampling to detect the potential interaction of loci with MS risk. Through re-analysis of the ANZgene dataset (1617 cases and 1988 controls) and an IMSGC dataset as a replication cohort (1313 cases and 1458 controls), we identified new association signals for MS predisposition, including SNPs above and below conventional significance thresholds while targeting two natural killer receptor loci and the well-established HLA loci. For example, rs2844482 (98.1% iterations), otherwise ignored by conventional statistics (p = 0.673) in the same dataset, was independently strongly associated with MS in another GWAS that required more than 40 times the number of cases (~45 K). Further comparison of our hits to those present in a large-scale meta-analysis, confirmed that the majority of SNPs identified by the elastic net model reached conventional statistical GWAS thresholds (p < 5 × 10−8 ) in this much larger dataset. Moreover, we found that gene variants involved in oxidative stress, in addition to innate immunity, were associated with MS. Overall, this study highlights the benefit of using more advanced statistical methods to (re-)analyse subtle genetic variation among loci that have a biological basis for their contribution to disease risk

Title: A CT-based intratumoral and peritumoral radiomics nomogram for postoperative recurrence risk stratification in localized clear cell renal cell carcinoma
Text source: abstract
Evidence text:
Abstract Objectives This study aimed to develop and validate a computed tomography (CT)-based intratumoral and peritumoral radiomics nomogram to improve the stratification of postoperative recurrence risk in patients with localized clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC). Methods This two-center study included 447 patients with localized ccRCC. Patients from Center A were randomly split into a training set (n = 281) and an internal validation set (IVS) (n = 114) in a 7:3 ratio, while 52 patients from Center B formed the external validation set (EVS). Radiomics features from preoperative CT were obtained from the internal area of tumor (IAT), the internal and peritumoral areas of the tumor at 3 mm (IPAT 3 mm), and 5 mm (IPAT 5 mm). The least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) Cox regression was used to construct a radiomics score to develop radiomics model (RM). A clinical model (CM) was also established using significant clinical factors. Furthermore, a fusion model (FM) was developed by integrating independent predictors from both clinical factors and the radiomics score (Radscore) through multivariate Cox proportional hazards regression. Model performance was assessed with Kaplan-Meier curves, time-dependent area under the curve (time-AUC), Harrell’s concordance index (C-index), and decision curve analysis (DCA). Results Compared to both the IAT model and the IPAT 3 mm model, the IPAT 5 mm radiomics model demonstrated superior predictive performance for tumor recurrence (C-index: 0.924 vs. 0.915–0.923 in the IVS; 0.952 vs. 0.920–0.944 in the EVS). Therefore, the IPAT 5 mm radiomics score was incorporated into the development of the fusion model. The FM exhibited outstanding predictive accuracy, achieving a C-index of 0.938 in the IVS, significantly outperforming the CM (0.889, P = 0.03). Notably, in the EVS, the RM surpassed both the CM and FM (C-index: 0.952 vs. 0.904–0.940, P > 0.05). Furthermore, decision curve analysis indicated that the FM provided the highest net clinical benefit in the IVS, while both the FM and RM demonstrated substantially greater net benefit than the CM in the EVS. Conclusions The radiomics model and the fusion model, which integrate both intratumoral and peritumoral features, offer accurate prediction of recurrence risk in patients with localized ccRCC. These models have the potential to aid in personalized treatment planning, optimized surveillance strategies, and treatment strategies for patients with clear cell renal cell carcinoma

Title: Silk Vista Baby for the treatment of distal anterior cerebral artery aneurysms
Text source: abstract
Evidence text:
Purpose: Treating small-caliber vessel aneurysms with flow diverters poses challenges due to narrow luminal diameters and tortuous vasculature, which complicate the navigation and deployment of conventional devices using standard microcatheters. The Silk Vista Baby (SVB, Balt, Montmorency, France) flow diverter was developed to treat intracranial aneurysms located in smaller vessels or more distal segments and is compatible with 0.017″ microcatheters. We present the largest multicenter analysis to date evaluating the outcomes of SVB use in unruptured distal anterior cerebral artery (DACA) aneurysms.

Methods: Retrospective data from 20 centers were reviewed for patients with unruptured DACA aneurysms treated with the SVB. Demographic information, clinical presentation, radiographic characteristics, complications, and outcomes were recorded.

Results: Seventy-nine patients (79 DACA aneurysms) were treated between January 2018 and December 2022; 59 were female (74.7%), and the median age was 61 years (IQR 53-67). Most aneurysms were saccular (89.9%), and 65.8% involved a branch. The median parent vessel diameter was 1.9 mm (IQR 1.7-2.1). A single stent was implanted in 97.5% of cases; 2.5% required two stents. The median imaging follow-up duration was 12 months (IQR 9.5-24). At the last follow-up, 76% of aneurysms showed complete or near-complete occlusion (O'Kelly-Marotta scale C or D, Raymond-Roy 1 or 2). Overall, thromboembolic or hemorrhagic complications occurred in 14% of patients, with two cases being symptomatic. The mortality rate was 0%, and the retreatment rate was 1.3%.

Published by BMJ Group.ABSTRACTObjective Food- related quality of life (FR- QoL) is the psychosocial impact of food, nutrition, eating and drinking on QoL and can be profoundly affected by inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). We aimed to translate and validate the FR- QoL- 29 Questionnaire in a Belgian IBD population and investigate associations with relevant clinical variables.Methods The English FR- QoL- 29 was translated to Dutch using the forward–backward method. Consecutive patients with IBD attending the outpatient clinic in a university hospital in Belgium completed the FR- QoL- 29 Dutch (Flemish), alongside questionnaires assessing disease severity and IBD- related disability. Clinical and biochemical data were collected. Exploratory factor analysis (EFA) with promax rotation assessed the underlying factor structure. Reliability measures (internal consistency, test–retest reliability) were evaluated. Pearson and Spearman correlations assessed relationships between FR- QoL- 29 Score and continuous demographic and clinical variables, while categorical parameters were analysed using independent t- tests and one- way analysis of variance with Tukey post hoc tests.Results 301 patients were included, with 31 (10.3%) completing the retest. EFA revealed a one- factor structure explaining 55% of the variance. The FR- QoL- 29- Dutch (Flemish) showed excellent internal consistency (Cronbach’s α=0.97) and very good test–retest reliability (intraclass correlation=0.94). Lower FR- QoL- 29 Score was associated with higher serum albumin levels, younger age, disease activity and IBD- related disability. FR- QoL- 29 Score was lower in females, those with Crohn’s disease (CD), CD patients with a stricturing phenotype and those previously receiving IBD- related surgery.Conclusion The FR- QoL- 29- Dutch (Flemish) is valid and reliable and correlates with disease activity and IBD- related disability. Patients with CD, stricturing disease and who previously underwent IBD- related surgery have a significantly lower FR- QoL and should be targeted for support.INTRODUCTIONInflammatory bowel diseases (IBD) are chronic diseases of the gastrointestinal tract, with Crohn’s disease (CD) and ulcerative colitis (UC) representing their main entities. IBD is now a global disease with compounding prevalence in Western countries, while incidence in developing nations is emerging and accelerating.1 Although genetic factors in IBD are important,2 environmental triggers such WHAT IS ALREADY KNOWN ON THIS TOPIC ⇒ Food- related quality of life (FR- QoL) encompasses the physical, emotional and social dimensions of eating and drinking and can be profoundly affected in inflammatory bowel disease (IBD).WHAT THIS STUDY ADDS ⇒ Here, we developed and validated the FR- QoL Questionnaire in Dutch, adapted to the Flemish setting. FR- QoL- 29 scores associated with serum albumin levels, age, sex, disease activity and IBD- related disability. FR- QoL was impaired in those with Crohn’s disease (CD), CD patients with a stric-turing phenotype and those previously receiving in-flammatory bowel disease- related surgery.HOW THIS STUDY MIGHT AFFECT RESEARCH, PRACTICE OR POLICY ⇒ The FR- QoL- 29- Dutch (Flemish) is valid and reliable and can be used in clinical and research settings. This study also highlights patient populations that should be targeted for support to improve food- related and overall QoL and impact on long- term (nutritional) outcomes.Protected by copyright, including for uses related to text and data mining, AI training, and similar technologies. . BMJ Open Gastroenterol 2025;12:e001940. doi:10.1136/bmjgast-2025-001940Open access as air pollution,3 smoking4 and diet5 are believed to explain the aforementioned trends.There is a key role for diet and nutritional manage-ment in IBD. There is evidence for a range of topics in general IBD management, from optimisation of nutri-tional status in preoperative patients and those at risk of malnutrition to treating inflammation and non- inflammatory symptoms.6 7 In addition to increasing interest from doctors and researchers, many patients also acknowledge the importance of nutrition as a part of their IBD experience. It was shown that 59% of patients with IBD value nutrition to be either more or equally important compared with medication, and 62% believe diet to be more important in influencing the disease course.8 Another study showed that as many as 92% of patients avoid one or more foods when experiencing active symptoms, and 74% continue to avoid doing so even in the absence of active symptoms.9Thus, food and diet appear to play an essential role in the management of IBD from both a patient and provider perspective. Further, the act of eating and drinking also fulfils psychosocial roles and brings joy to people’s lives. This idea, known as ‘food- related quality of life’ (FR- QoL), includes the physical, emotional and social aspects of eating and drinking and their influence on overall well- being.10–12 The FR- QoL- 29, a question-naire assessing FR- QoL in patients with IBD, was devel-oped by Hughes et al in patients with IBD from the UK. This disease- specific, validated instrument includes 29 items that assess the psychosocial aspects of eating and drinking in IBD.10–12 Studies have subsequently shown that clinical factors such as active disease and severe symptoms, history of IBD surgery, anxiety and depres-sion and restrictive eating behaviour may influence FR- QoL.13 In addition, in the largest cohort to date, also from the UK, poorer FR- QoL is associated with a lower intake of important nutrients, including those relating to gut health and bone mineralisation.12 Further, another study found that a poorer FR- QoL is associated with malnutrition risk.14 Together, these data suggest a very complex and perhaps even bidirectional relation-ship between the nutritional status of patients with IBD and corresponding FR- QoL.While cohorts in English- speaking countries are now well characterised and include patients with IBD from the UK,10 12 15 USA,16–18 Australia,19 and New Zealand,20 studies from Europe are limited to Portugal,21 Turkey,14 and a small paediatric trial in Romania,22 the latter using an unvalidated version of the questionnaire. Since socio-cultural influences can heavily affect FR- QoL,23 data from various regions are of interest, with a current blind spot at the North European mainland. In addition, most avail-able cohorts to date lack biochemical data. Therefore, we aimed to (1) translate and validate a Dutch version of the FR- QoL- 29 for IBD, adapted to the Flemish setting and to (2) identify IBD- related factors that may associate with the FR- QoL, including demographic and clinical charac-teristics as well as biochemical elements.METHODSDutch translation of the FR-QoL-29Permission to translate the original version of the FR- QoL- 29 was granted by the copyright holders (King’s College London). The translation and adaptation of the UK- developed instrument was done using the forward–backward method according to the published guidelines for cross- cultural healthcare research.24 Specif-ically, forward translation was performed by two indepen-dent researchers consisting of one IBD specialist fluent in both English and Dutch and one certified linguist who works as a translator in healthcare. Next, backward trans-lation was performed by two independent researchers, of which one was a bilingual IBD specialist and the other a linguist, but without a background in healthcare. After each step, both versions were compared, and discrep-ancies were resolved. Lastly, through collaboration with the Flemish IBD patient organisation (Crohn en Colitis ulcerosa Vereniging vzw), 10 patients were asked to rate the instructions and specific questions using a dichoto-mous scale (clear or unclear), also providing more detail when (part of) an item was deemed unclear. Suggestions on how to improve our questions were also welcomed. When at least 20% of patients rated a question as unclear, that question was re- evaluated by the research team, after which the final questionnaire was constructed; the FR- QoL- 29- Dutch (Flemish).Study populationConsecutive patients with confirmed CD or UC who were attending the outpatient clinic of the University Hospitals Leuven on days that members of the study team were present between October 2023 and July 2024 were invited to participate in the current study. Eligible patients attended standard of care clinical appointments, including appointments at the infusion clinic to receive intravenous IBD therapies, and patients presenting at the outpatient clinic for scheduled clinical follow- up visits. No patients were included who presented for endos-copy, surgery or unscheduled care at the emergency department. Only adult patients with a good under-standing of Dutch were included. As per our standard of care, all included patients were seen during routine follow- up and received questions about their disease activity patient- reported outcome (PRO)- 2 and Mani-toba Inflammatory Bowel Disease Index (MIBDI)) and QoL (Inflammatory Bowel Disease Disability Index (IBD Disk)) through the digital health records. In addition, we used chart review to collect demographic data (age and sex), medical history (diagnosis (UC/CD), time since diagnosis (years), Montreal classification (for UC: E extent of disease and for CD: A age at diagnosis, B disease behaviour type and L location), IBD- related surgical history (yes/no), previous and current IBD- related ther-apies, use of neuromodulators and smoking), as well as anthropometric data (length, body weight and body mass index (BMI)), and available laboratory data including biochemical blood results (C reactive protein (CRP), Protected by copyright, including for uses related to text and data mining, AI training, and similar technologies. . We also assessed whether patients received advanced IBD- related treatments, including biological treatments and small molecules, which we hereafter refer to as ‘advanced status’. Therefore, to assess clinical status, several disease severity indices were used to capture as many IBD- related aspects as possible from a holistic point of view.To meet general criteria for both exploratory and confirmatory factor analysis, a target sample size of at least 300 patients with IBD was set to validate the trans-lated FR- QoL- 29- Dutch (Flemish). To assess test–retest reliability as a measure of internal validity, a subset of 10% of the included population was asked to complete the questionnaire again, between 1 and 2 weeks after the first questionnaire was filled in. The first 10% of patients who agreed to this were selected for this part of the study and contacted by telephone to collect replies.QuestionnairesFR- QoL- Dutch (Flemish): This is a 29- item self- report measure designed to assess the psychosocial impact of food, diet, eating and drinking on various daily living domains, specifically validated for patients with IBD who are Dutch (Flemish) speaking. Each item is rated on a 5- point Likert scale, ranging from 1 (strongly agree) to 5 (strongly disagree), resulting in a score range from 5 to 145. Higher scores indicate greater FR- QoL.MIBDI: The MIBDI is a single- item, patient- reported tool that assesses perceived disease activity over the past 6 months.25 Patients are asked to rate their disease activity on a 5- point scale, with response options ranging from ‘not active at all’ to ‘extremely active’. Higher scores indi-cate greater perceived disease severity.CD- PRO- 2: The CD- PRO- 2 is a self- report measure of disease activity in patients with CD and a subscore of the Crohn’s Disease Activity Index.26 The CD- PRO- 2 includes two items: one assessing stool frequency (ie, number of liquid or soft stools per day) and the other assessing abdominal pain (0=none, 1=mild, 2=moderate, 3=severe) over a 7- day period. Scores are calculated by summing the values of these two components, with higher scores indicating greater disease severity.UC- PRO- 2: The UC- PRO- 2 is a self- reported measure of disease activity for patients with UC.27 Adapted from the Mayo Clinic Score, the UC- PRO- 2 includes two items: one assessing stool frequency (0=normal number of stools, 1=1–2 stools above normal, 2=3–4 stools above normal, 3=5 or more stools above normal) and another assessing rectal bleeding (0=none, 1=visible blood with stool less than half the time, 2=visible blood with stool half the time or more, 3=passing blood alone), based on symptoms over the previous 3 days. Higher scores indi-cate greater disease severity.IBD Disk: The IBD Disk is a 10- item self- report question-naire that evaluates IBD- related disability across multiple domains, including abdominal pain, defecation, inter-personal interactions, education and work, sleep, energy, emotions, body image, sexual functioning and joint pain.28 Responses are rated on a 10- point scale, ranging from 0 (absolutely disagree) to 10 (absolutely agree). Higher scores indicate greater IBD- related disability.The Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology reporting guideline was followed to report our findings (online supplemental table 1).Statistical analysisAll statistical analyses were performed using RStudio (V.2024.04.2). Descriptive statistics were calculated to summarise the data, with means and SD for continuous variables and frequencies and percentages for categorical variables. Histograms and the Shapiro- Wilk normality test were employed to assess the normality of the data. For variables that did not meet the assumption of normality, log- transformation was applied as necessary. In addition, Pearson and Spearman correlations (as appropriate) were used to assess relationships between FR- QoL and relevant demographic and clinical variables, including age, BMI, time since diagnosis, faecal calprotectin, CRP and serum albumin. Independent samples t- tests were conducted to assess differences in FR- QoL between sexes. Missing data were handled using pairwise deletion to maximise the use of available data.The original FR- QoL- 29 validation study identified a four- factor model, with items loading across four distinct factors. However, each item also loaded onto the first factor, representing general aspects of FR- QoL. Conse-quently, the authors opted to interpret the FR- QoL- 29 as a unidimensional construct. Based on this, we conducted an exploratory factor analysis (EFA) to examine the ques-tionnaire’s factor structure without imposing a predeter-mined model structure. The Kaiser- Meyer- Olkin (KMO) test and Bartlett’s test of sphericity were conducted to assess the suitability of the data for factor analysis.29–31 The KMO test measures the proportion of variance in the variables that may be attributed to underlying factors, indicating the appropriateness of factor analysis. The KMO statistic ranges from 0 to 1, with higher values suggesting a stronger suitability for factor analysis. Typi-cally, a KMO value above 0.6 is considered acceptable, with values closer to 1 indicating greater adequacy. Bart-lett’s test of sphericity evaluated whether the correlation matrix was significantly different from an identity matrix, ensuring that the variables were sufficiently interrelated to justify factor extraction.Eigenvalues and parallel analysis, along with a scree plot, were used to determine the initial number of factors to extract. Eigenvalues greater than 1 were considered as a preliminary criterion for factor retention, while parallel analysis compared the observed eigenvalues to those obtained from randomly generated data to iden-tify meaningful factors. The accompanying scree plot provided a visual representation of the eigenvalues, with the ‘elbow point’ indicating where the curve levelled off, suggesting the optimal number of factors to retain. We applied a polychoric correlation to account for the ordinal nature of the data (eg, Likert scale responses).32Reliability was assessed using multiple measures, including internal consistency, split- half reliability and test–retest reliability. Internal consistency was evalu-ated using Cronbach’s alpha to determine how well the items within the questionnaire were correlated and measured the same underlying construct. Split- half reli-ability, assessed using Guttman’s statistic, examined the consistency of responses between two halves of the ques-tionnaire. Test–retest reliability was measured by adminis-tering the questionnaire at two different time points and calculating the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) to assess the stability and reproducibility of responses over time. Convergent validity was assessed by examining correlations between FR- QoL- Dutch and measures of disease severity (Manitoba IBD Index, PRO- 2) and IBD- related disability (IBD Disk). Clinical factor differences (IBD type (CD/UC), surgical history (yes/no), neuro-modulator use (yes/no), receiving advanced therapies (yes/no), montreal IBD classification for CD A (A1/A2/A3), CD B (B1/B2/B3), CD L (L1/L2/L3/L4) and UC (E1/E2/E3)), as well as biochemical data including CRP and albumin were analysed using independent samples t- tests and one- way analysis of variance (ANOVA) with Tukey post hoc tests as appropriate.RESULTSSample characteristicsA total of 301 participants completed the FR- QoL- Dutch (Flemish), with 31 (10.3%) participating at two time-points for measurement of test–retest reliability. The average age of participants was 45.2±15.4 years, with 51.8% (n=156) male. The majority (n=201, 66.8%) of participants were diagnosed with CD. Full demographic and clinical information is presented in table 1. The mean FR- QoL- 29 total score in our cohort was 86.3 (SD 24.6).Exploratory factor analysis (EFA)The KMO test yielded a measure of sampling adequacy of 0.94, and Bartlett’s Test of Sphericity was significant (p<0.0001), both indicating that the data were suitable for factor analysis. Eigenvalues suggested a four- factor model, while parallel analysis indicated a five- factor model. Further, the one- factor model has routinely validated across many samples. Therefore, EFA was conducted on three different models: a five- factor, four- factor and one- factor model. The five- factor model explained 68% of the variance; however, the fifth factor contained only two items and several items cross- loaded, suggesting that five factors might be too many to delin-eate distinct constructs (online supplemental table 2). Finally, the one- factor model explained 55% of the variance (table 2), and all items loaded strongly on the single factor. As a result, it was determined to proceed with the one- factor model.ReliabilityThe FR- QoL- 29- Dutch (Flemish) showed excellent internal consistency (Cronbach’s α=0.97), strong split- half reliability (Guttman Lambda- 6=0.98) and very good test–retest reliability (ICC=0.94 (95% CI: 0.88 to 0.97)).Association between FR-QoL and demographic, clinical and biochemical parametersFR- QoL- 29 total scores differed significantly between sexes (t- test, n=301, p=0.0001), with women (mean score (M) = 80.7, SD=22.0) reporting significantly lower values compared with men (M=91.5, SD=25.9, (online supple-mental figure 1). FR- QoL was significantly different by disease type (t- test, n=301, p=0.01) (figure 1A), with lower scores reported in patients with CD (M=83.9, SD=24.3) compared with UC (M=91.3, SD=24.6). Further, differ-ences existed by surgical history (t- test, n=300, p=0.0001) (figure 1B) and w lower in patients with a history of IBD- related surgery (M=80.2, SD=23.6) compared with surgery- naive patients (M=91.0, SD=24.3). Among patients with CD (n=201), a one- way ANOVA was conducted to examine the effect of Montreal behaviour classification (B1, B2, B3) on FR- QoL independent of surgical history, which showed a significant effect (p=0.002) (figure 1C). Post hoc Tukey’s HSD tests indicated that CD patients with stricturing disease (B2) had significantly lower FR- QoL- 29 total scores (M=74.7, SD=19.8) than those with non- stricturing, non- penetrating disease (B1, M=87.7, SD=23.4; p=0.003) and penetrating disease (B3, M=87.9, SD=28.0; p=0.015). There was no significant difference between B1 and B3 (p=0.999). Additionally, FR- QoL29 total scores did not differ by age of onset (Montreal CD A; p=0.30), disease location in CD (Montreal CD L; p=0.51), or disease extension in UC (Montreal UC E; p=0.87), advanced therapy (p=0.77), or neuromodulator use (p=0.09) (online supplemental figures 2A–4).As expected, higher FR- QoL- 29 total scores were significantly and negatively correlated with measures of self- reported disease activity (Manitoba: Spearman’s rho, n=165, rs = −0.49, p<0.0001; CD- PRO- 2: Pearson’s correla-tion, n=105, r = −0.48, p<0.0001); UC- PRO- 2: Spearman’s rho, n=52, rs = −0.43, p=0.001); and IBD- related disability (Pearson’s correlation, n=133, r = −0.54, p<0.0001; Online supplemental figure 5A–6). Further, FR- QoL- 29 scores were significantly positively correlated, though weakly, with serum albumin levels (Spearman’s rank, n=279, rs=0.13, p=0.03) and a borderline significant inverse correlation was found between FR- QoL- 29 scores and age (Spearman’s rank, n=301, rs=−0.11, p=0.05) (online supplemental figures 7 and 8). FR- QoL- 29 total scores were not significantly associated with any additional demographic, clinical (eg, BMI, time since diagnosis), or biochemical parameters (eg, faecal calprotectin, CRP).DISCUSSIONThis is the first study to validate a Dutch FR- QoL Ques-tionnaire for IBD, adapted to the Flemish culture, using a standardised methodology in an adequately powered cohort.24 Consistent with other studies, our analysis found that a one- factor model structure appropriately fit the data, providing further evidence for a unidi-mensional construct. We demonstrate for the first time that stricturing disease is significantly associated with decreased FR- QoL compared with an inflammatory and a penetrating disease type. This expands previous find-ings in the Portuguese cohort showing better FR- QoL in inflammatory subtypes compared with other subtypes. In addition, we are the first to show a positive association between serum albumin levels and FR- QoL, elaborating on the findings from the USA cohort from Florida, where FR- QoL- 29 scores in CD were positively correlated with haemoglobin and iron levels.18 We also confirm previous findings that FR- QoL correlates with disease activity10 15 16 and IBD- related disability12 and is poorer in women18 and in those who underwent surgery.14 In addition, we show that patients with CD have significantly worse FR- QoL, which is only partly in line with previous reports.22The mean score in our cohort was 86.3 (SD 24.6), which is markedly lower than the reported scores in Portugal and Turkey and more comparable to the Anglo- Saxon countries (online supplemental table 4). In addition, as sampling was performed in the outpatient clinic, a wide range of disease phenotypes and patients treated with a variety of drugs were included. Since data collection was based on standard of care protocols, we were able to study determining factors through clinical characteristics based on physician notes, as well as biochemical param-eters and questionnaires on IBD- related disability and overall QoL.We do acknowledge certain limitations. First, all patients were recruited from a tertiary care hospital, which might lead to referral bias and most probably a case mix consisting of more severe and complex cases, which is likely to skew the reported FR- QoL scores towards lower values. Now that a tool is available to measure FR- QoL in our Dutch- speaking population, further research in regional hospi-tals can be performed to test this hypothesis. Second, as this study was primarily a validation study, the recruitment was pragmatic and thus response rates were not formally collected. This might result in a sampling bias, potentially affecting our results. Along this line, as data on Patient Reported Outcome Measures (PROMs) and other assess-ment tools on QoL were recorded through electronic questionnaires that are delivered as the standard of care protocol, response rates were between 45.2% and 55.8%. Although these response rates are to be expected from this type of data collection,35 missing data might also impact our results on this front. Third, although we acknowledge that the time since surgical intervention may influence FR- QoL, we were unable in the present study to account for this, and future research should investigate this further. Fourth, we did not assess the effect of receiving dietetic counselling or following a specific diet (either self- imposed or prescribed), and likewise, we currently do not know whether a restrictive diet could affect FR- QoL scores. As current evidence somewhat counter- intuitively suggests that dietary therapy and nutritional counselling is associated with a poorer FR- QoL, potentially due to reverse causality, future studies are needed to elucidate the role of non- inflammatory symptoms and dietetic counselling to elucidate the directionality of this associ-ation.16 17 21 In addition, as avoidant eating behaviours are common in IBD patients, even when in clinical remis-sion and could impact FR- QoL, screening for disordered eating (ie, anorexia nervosa and avoidant- restrictive food intake disorder) should be considered in future proj-ects.9 36 Together, these data suggest that FR- QoL might be crucially important in delivering future dietary inter-ventional studies and that this could even be considered as an endpoint alongside clinical remission. In addition, this highlights the importance of delivering nutritional counselling by appropriately trained dietitians. Title: Multi-Objective Multi-Gene Genetic Programming for the Prediction of Leakage in Water Distribution Networks
Text source: abstract
Evidence text:
Understanding leakage is an important challenge within the water sector to minimise waste, energy use and carbon emissions. Every Water Distribution Network (WDN) has leakage, usually approximated as Minimum Night Flow (MNF) for each District Metered Area (DMA). However, not all DMAs have instruments to monitor leakage directly, or the main dynamic factors that contribute to it. Therefore, this article will estimate the leakage of a DMA by using the recorded features of its pipes, making use of readily available asset data collected routinely by water companies. This article interprets this problem as a feature construction task and uses a multi-objective multi-gene strongly typed genetic programming approach to create a set of features. These features are used by a linear regression model to estimate the average long-term leakage in DMAs and Shapley values are used to understand the impact and importance of each tree. The methodology is applied to a dataset for a real-world WDN with over 700 DMAs and the results are compared to a previous work which used human-constructed features. The results show comparable performance with significantly fewer, and less complex features. In addition, novel features are found that were not part of the human-constructed features

Convergence of Unregularized Online Learning Algorithms
Yunwen Lei∗1, Lei Shi†2 and Zheng-Chu Guo‡3
1Department of Mathematics, City University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong, China

August 11, 2017
Abstract
In this paper we study the convergence of online gradient descent algorithms in reproducing
kernel Hilbert spaces (RKHSs) without regularization. We establish a sufficient condition and
a necessary condition for the convergence of excess generalization errors in expectation. A
sufficient condition for the almost sure convergence is also given. With high probability, we
provide explicit convergence rates of the excess generalization errors for both averaged iterates
and the last iterate, which in turn also imply convergence rates with probability one. To our
best knowledge, this is the first high-probability convergence rate for the last iterate of online
gradient descent algorithms without strong convexity. Without any boundedness assumptions
on iterates, our results are derived by a novel use of two measures of the algorithm’s one-step
progress, respectively by generalization errors and by distances in RKHSs, where the variances
of the involved martingales are cancelled out by the descent property of the algorithm.
Keywords: Learning theory, Online learning, Convergence analysis, Reproducing kernel
Hilbert space
1 Introduction
Online gradient descent is a scalable method able to tackle large-scale data arriving in a sequen-
tial manner [8, 10, 14, 37], which is becoming ubiquitous within the big data era. As a first-order
method, it iteratively builds an unbiased estimate of the true gradient upon the arrival of a new
example and uses this information to guide the learning process [37, 39]. As verified by theoreti-
cal and empirical analysis, online gradient descent enjoys comparable performance as compared to
its batch counterpart such as gradient descent [24, 32, 37], while attaining a great computational
speed-up since its gradient calculation involves only a single example. As a comparison, the gradient
calculation in gradient descent requires to traverse all training examples. Recently, online gradient
descent has received renewed attention due to the wide applications of its stochastic analogue, i.e.,
stochastic gradient descent, in training deep neural networks [2, 21, 30].
In this paper, we are interested in the setting that training examples {zt = (xt, yt)}t∈N are

Despite its widespread applications, the theoretical understanding of the online gradient descent
algorithms are still not satisfactory in the following three aspects. Firstly, boundedness assumptions
on the iterates are often imposed in the literature, which may be violated in practical implementa-
tions if the underlying domain is not bounded. Although a projection of iterates onto a bounded
domain guarantees the boundedness assumption, the projection operator may be time-consuming
and this introduces an additional challenging problem of tuning the size of the domain. Secondly,
most of the theoretical results are stated in expectation, while we are sometimes more interested
in either almost sure convergence or convergence rates with high probability. Indeed, an algorithm
may suffer from a high variability and should be used with caution if neither almost sure convergence
nor high-probability bounds hold [25]. In particular, an almost sure convergence is still lacking for
online gradient descent algorithms applied to general convex problems [36]. Lastly, most existing
convergence rates are stated for some average of iterates. Though taking average of iterates can
improve the robustness of the solution [20], it can either destroy the sparsity of the solution which
is crucial for a proper interpretation of models in many applications, or slow down the training
speed in practical implementations [22].
In this paper, we aim to take a further step to tackle the above mentioned problems. We establish
a general sufficient condition and a necessary condition on the step sizes for the convergence of online
gradient descent algorithms in expectation. With Doob’s martingale convergence theorem and the
Borel-Cantelli lemma, a sufficient condition for the almost sure convergence and explicit convergence
rates with probability one are also established. Furthermore, we present high-probability bounds
for both averaged iterates and the last iterate of online gradient descent algorithms. To our best
knowledge, this is the first high-probability convergence rate for the last iterate of online gradient
descent algorithms in the general convex setting. Our analysis does not impose any boundedness
assumptions on the iterates. Indeed, we show that, although implemented in an unbounded domain,
the iterates produced by (1.1) fall into a bounded domain with high probability (up to logarithmic
factors). Our analysis is performed by viewing the one-step progress of online gradient descent
algorithms from different yet unified perspectives: one in terms of generalization errors and one in
terms of RKHS distances. For both viewpoints, we relate the one-step progress to a martingale
difference sequence and a negative term due to the descent nature of the algorithm. Our novelty is
to show that the dominant variance term appearing in the application of a Bernstein-type inequality
to these martingales can be cancelled out by the negative terms in the one-step progress inequalities.
Both viewpoints of the one-step progress are indispensable in our analysis.
The remaining parts of this paper are organized as follows. We present main results in Section
2. Discussions and comparisons with related work are given in Section 3. The proofs of main results
are given in Section 4.

Machine Learning of Molecular Electronic Properties in Chemical Compound Space
Gre´goire Montavon,1 Matthias Rupp,2 Vivekanand Gobre,3 Alvaro Vazquez-Mayagoitia,4 Katja
Hansen,3 Alexandre Tkatchenko,3, 5, ∗ Klaus-Robert Mu¨ller,1, 6, † and O. Anatole von Lilienfeld4, ‡
1Machine Learning Group, Technical University of Berlin, Franklinstr 28/29, 10587 Berlin, Germany
2Institute of Pharmaceutical Sciences, ETH Zurich, 8093 Zu¨rich, Switzerland
3Fritz-Haber-Institut der Max-Planck-Gesellschaft, 14195 Berlin, Germany

5Department of Chemistry, Pohang University of Science and Technology, Pohang 790–784, Korea
